The analysis of retrieved implants and periprosthetic tissue is an important tool for the
retrospective evaluation of the in vivo performance of orthopaedic implants. In general,
two types of retrievals must be distinguished: surgical retrievals and postmortem or
autopsy retrievals.1 Surgical retrievals are performed for cause during revision surgery.
The reasons for revision include infection, instability, implant fracture, accelerated wear,
osteolysis, aseptic loosening, adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR), and other reasons,
depending on the type of joint and prosthesis. A thorough retrieval analysis will help to
confirm or accurately determine the reason for failure. Histopathologic analysis of the
periprosthetic tissue will determine if implant debris, such as polyethylene and metal
particles from the bearing surfaces, or tribocorrosion products from modular junctions
or secondary interfaces (eg, backside wear) caused a tissue response associated with
osteolysis or characteristic lymphocyte-dominated ALTR. The latter can occur, especially
about total hip arthroplasty implants and easily can be misdiagnosed as an infection
without appropriate histopathologic evaluation (Resources 1 and 2).
Analysis of surgically retrieved implants is important because it can provide knowledge
of potential material or structural failure of the implant. Failure analysis focuses on three
main types of material related failures: wear, fatigue, and corrosion. Wear, which is the
subject of the field of tribology, is inherent to load-bearing joints but may be excessive
under adverse conditions (eg, malalignment) and ultimately may lead to an adverse
response or, in some patients, structural failure.2 Although implants are designed and
preclinically tested to withstand fatigue-related fracture, fracture can result from
overloading, nonunion of fractures or fusions, malalignment, or flaws within the
material. For example, a small flaw within the material or on the surface (deep scratch)
may be the location of crack initiation and propagation. If a fracture occurs, retrieval
analysis can accurately determine the cause, based on damage features within the
fracture surfaces. Corrosion of orthopaedic implants should be minimized by the choice
of a metal alloy with excellent corrosion resistance, such as titanium alloys, cobalt-
chromium-molybdenum (CoCrMo) alloy, and stainless steels. All these alloys generally
are protected by a thin oxide film—also known as passive film—that is stable under
static conditions and prevents corrosion. However, corrosion and fretting corrosion may
result from crevices provided by modular junctions and from unexpected changes within
the chemical and electrochemical conditions in vivo.3-8 Retrieval analysis can provide

information about corrosion modes that occurred in vivo, how corrosion may be related
to flaws within the alloy, and what types of corrosion products are produced.9,10
The analysis of postmortem retrieved implants may provide valuable information.11
Dissimilar from surgical retrievals, these implants never needed to be removed and,
therefore, can be considered as a well-functioning control group.1,12,13 The answer to
why these implants worked well is just as important as the answer to why other implants
did not work well. In addition, postmortem retrievals allow for the study of local and
remote bone and soft tissue to address other long-term performance variables, such as
implant osseointegration and dissemination of implant debris, and potential systemic
effects.14-16 Although the establishment and maintenance of a repository of surgically
retrieved implants requires considerable effort and resources, a postmortem retrieval
program is more challenging in this regard. Therefore, only a few research groups have
this capability.
Terms and Definitions
Particle-Induced Osteolysis

Particle-Induced Osteolysis
Osteolysis is the pathologic destruction of bone tissue. Particle-induced osteolysis results
from an inflammatory reaction to an abundance of wear and corrosion debris, which is
characterized histopathologically as masses of particle-laden macrophages. This process
engages osteoclasts to increase bone resorption and osteoblasts to reduce bone
formation. It may lead to implant loosening, periprosthetic fracture, and pain.15,17-19
ALTR/Aseptic Lymphocyte-Dominated Vasculitis-Associated
Lesions/Adverse Reaction to Metal
Debris/Pseudotumor/Metallosis/Trunnionosis


ALTR/Aseptic Lymphocyte-Dominated Vasculitis-Associated
Lesions/Adverse Reaction to Metal
Debris/Pseudotumor/Metallosis/Trunnionosis
Various terms are used in the orthopaedic literature to describe the tissue reactions and
lesions associated with severe implant wear and corrosion of metal/metal modular
junctions and metal-on-metal (MOM) bearings. ALTR, aseptic lymphocyte-dominated
vasculitis-associated lesions (ALVAL), pseudotumor, metallosis, and trunnionosis are
among the names erroneously used interchangeably as a descriptor and/or diagnosis,
leading to confusion and imprecision. Pseudotumor is a clinical and imaging descriptor
referring to benign, aseptic fluid-filled soft-tissue masses associated with an implant with
a cystic wall of variable thickness. ALVAL is a histologic description based on the
presence of large masses of lymphocytes adjacent to blood vessels. It is similar to but
not pathognomonic of a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. The degree of ALVAL can
be scored via a method involving semi-quantification of cell and tissue types present
within the lesions.20 ALVAL is not a clinical diagnosis. Pseudotumor and ALVAL are terms
used extensively and imprecisely in association with failed MOM components.20-22
Trunnionosis and metallosis are descriptive terms derived from gross observations
during revision surgery. Trunnionosis refers to tribocorrosion damage at the femoral
head-neck junction,23 whereas metallosis describes the stained appearance of the joint
capsule and periprosthetic tissues caused by large amounts of metal debris. The cellular
response to this type of debris may vary widely. ALTR is best defined as a variable
combination of benign aseptic masses (pseudotumors), ALVAL, soft- and hard-tissue
necrosis, and osteolysis in proximity to a joint implant. Adverse reaction to metal debris
also is used to describe cellular and tissue reactions in the periprosthetic tissue and in
remote tissues; however, no set convention for the use of this terminology exists, and
care should be taken to use it appropriately.24
Tribology
Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion. This field covers wear, friction,
and lubrication.

Tribosystem
A tribosystem consists of the bearing couple (body and counter body), the intermediate fluid,
and the surrounding environment.
Tribocorrosion
Tribocorrosion is deterioration or transformation of material via simultaneous action of wear
and corrosion.
Fretting
Fretting is the wear process of two interacting surfaces undergoing cyclic micromotion.
Micromotion occurs if the relative motion amplitude is smaller than the diameter of the
contact area.
Fretting Corrosion
Fretting corrosion is tribocorrosion processes that occur under fretting
Implant Retrieval Analysis
From the Operating Room to the Laboratory
Implants retrieved during revision surgery will be sent postoperatively to pathology along with
a representative sample of periprosthetic tissue. Tissue samples will be analyzed to finalize the
determination of the cause of failure, especially whether infection occurred. Pathologic
analysis of implants most often is limited to a rudimentary description of the implants
received, with the amount of detail given varying with each pathologist. In most cases, the
implant will be discarded after a period of a few weeks if the patient does not request the
implant.
The protocol for how long implants are kept varies among hospitals and medical centers.
Additional retrieval analyses can be performed on a case basis or as part of an ongoing
retrieval repository. The latter requires Institutional Review Board approval and considerable
logistic efforts.
Under any circumstance, retrieved implants must be disinfected on additional analysis.
Although sterilization may have occurred in pathology before receiving the implant, retrieved

implants should be disinfected to ensure the elimination of biohazards. To protect patient
privacy, implants brought into the laboratory should be given a unique laboratory
identification number, and any patient information should be secured with access limited to
key study personnel. Before microscopic analysis, visual inspection and cleaning must be
performed because retrieved implants may be covered by different types and extents of
organic residue and implant debris. The extent of cleaning depends on the study goals. Photo
documentation of implant surfaces before each cleaning step is recommended.
For the analysis of biofilms or tribofilms formed in situ,25,26 starting with incremental
conservative cleaning methods (eg, cleaning with the use of a soft toothbrush and running
water) is recommended.
To evaluate damage features on implant bearing surfaces or corrosion sites, more severe
cleaning methods, such as sonication and enzymatic soaps, may be used.
Wear Modes, Mechanisms, and Features
From an engineering standpoint, total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA)
implants are technical bearings that will undergo wear by design during the normal course of
their lifetime. Although the goal is to minimize the generation of wear debris, no joint
replacement material couple currently can prevent wear entirely.
The amount of wear generated by a specific implant material strongly depends on the acting
wear mode. The term wear mode has two different meanings: one in the orthopaedic implant
research community and another in the field of tribology in general. Both meanings are
important to understand and provide essential guidance for retrieval analysis.
The first meaning was established by McKellop,27 who defined different wear modes
depending on potential in vivo deviations of the intended function of the prosthesis. The types
of wear mode can differ between implant types; however, in general, four different wear
modes can be distinguished.
Wear mode 1 is defined as the intended use, in which only the two actual bearing surfaces
are in contact as designed. Under this wear mode, material loss should match preclinical
testing results fairly well (eg, femoral head articulating with a polyethylene liner).
Wear mode 2 describes the contact of a bearing surface against a nonbearing surface, which
can occur under micro-separation in the hip or subluxation. This unintended contact may
lead to more severe damage (eg, stripe wear, a wear scar formed from micro-separation of
the femoral head from the liner, leading to cyclically occurring severe contact between the
head bearing surface and the rim of the liner).28

Wear mode 3 is the so-called three-body wear, which is characterized by the presence of
hard particles in between the two bearing surfaces. Particles may originate from the outside
(eg, bone, metal debris from surgical tools) or from the implant itself (eg, hard particles
generated from bearing surface wear).
Wear mode 4 is defined as the contact between two nonbearing surfaces. In THA implants,
this may be impingement wear, in which the femoral neck is in contact with the rim of the
acetabular cup, or backside wear between the acetabular liner and cup. Backside wear also
frequently occurs in TKA implants between the tibial liners and the tibial tray.29
In the field of tribology, the term wear mode defines the general mechanical conditions under
which a bearing is operating. Therefore, a wear mode is determined by (1) the macroscopic
structure of the tribosystem and the kinematic interaction of its elements and (2) the
combined effect of its underlying wear mechanisms.2 Under this definition, wear modes differ,
depending on the bearing type. For example, the intended wear mode (wear mode 1) differs
between THA and TKA. By design, THA implants undergo a wear mode of sliding wear because
both bearing surfaces are conforming. If hard particles (eg, bone cement) enter the
tribosystem, the wear mode will transition to three-body sliding wear. Conversely, TKA
implants exhibit nonconforming bearing surfaces and a more complex kinematic situation
because of the overlapping motions of flexion/extension, adduction/abduction, and
internal/external rotation. The resulting wear mode is a combination of sliding wear and rolling
wear. The presence of rolling wear enables a different wear mechanism because of stress
concentration in the subsurface area of the polyethylene liner.
The term wear mechanism describes and distinguishes different mechanical and chemical
interactions between bearing surfaces. In general, four different wear mechanisms exist:
adhesion, abrasion, surface fatigue, and tribochemical reactions; however, some sub-
mechanisms also exist. The determination of which wear mechanisms occurred can be made
via retrieval analysis with the observation of specific wear features.
Wear features may differ broadly among various implant materials, material couples, and the
acting wear mechanism.
Under normal conditions, a metal-on-polyethylene or ceramic-on-polyethylene THA implant
mainly exhibits wear of the polyethylene liner. The acting wear mechanisms are known to be
adhesive and abrasive wear.2,30-32 The resulting wear scar is mainly characterized by
polishing and fine scratches. Three-body wear is known to occur, especially via the
introduction of bone cement debris. The result may be deeper scratches or grooves and
embedded cement debris. If cement debris is removed from the surface, it leaves shallow

pits that may be confused with pitting caused by surface fatigue; however, pits from cement
debris can be distinguished by material built up at one side of the individual pits. In TKA
implants, a larger variety of wear features have been observed depending on polyethylene
liner geometry and the type of polyethylene material. Wear features were first described by
Hood et al33 and were expanded on by others over time.34,35 These common features
include polishing, burnishing, scratching, pitting, embedded cement debris, a striated
pattern, and delamination. In the past, polyethylene liners were known to exhibit
delamination, which is the result of severe surface fatigue that commonly occurs under
rolling wear.12,36 Subsurface stresses lead to cracks that propagate under cyclic load parallel
to the surface, resulting in the detachment of large flakes, which leave behind large oddly
shaped wear scars and discoloration. In severe cases, this may lead to fracture. The
occurrence of delamination has been almost eliminated via the introduction of highly cross-
linked and vitamin-E doped polyethylene. By substantially reducing oxidation, these
contemporary materials are less prone to crack propagation. Even conventional polyethylene
that is sterilized in an inert environment is substantially less prone to delamination than
historic polyethylene that was sterilized in air.12,32,37,38 The introduction of highly cross-
linked polyethylene has resulted in decreased wear and a decreased risk of osteolysis
because of improved tribologic properties.39,40
Wear features on ceramic surfaces occur in ceramic-on-ceramic THA implants; however,
under well-functioning conditions, this material couple exhibits the lowest wear volume.
Wear occurs under adverse contact conditions, such as micro-separation and edge loading.
Both may lead to so-called stripe wear,28,41-43 which is characterized by a stripe of severe
wear across the femoral head and a corresponding wear scar close to the rim of the
acetabular cup. Depending on whether stripe wear is caused by severe contact (micro-
separation) or disruption of lubricating film formation, fractured ceramic grains or fracture
along grain boundaries and subsequent grain pullout will be observed.44 In both cases, hard
particles detach from the surface and may introduce additional three-body wear. Stipe wear
on ceramic bearings also often is connected with an audible squeaking noise that is
bothersome to patients.45-47 The occurrence of stripe wear is unlikely in ceramic-on-
polyethylene bearings; however, ceramic wear can occur if subluxation, even temporarily,
causes contact between ceramic and metal surfaces. If a ceramic-on-ceramic or ceramic-on-
polyethylene THA implant needs to be revised, it should only be replaced with another
ceramic bearing surface and not a metal bearing surface. Even a few ceramic particles
entering the interface may cause devastating three-body wear to the metal surface or embed

within the polyethylene surface, accelerating abrasive wear of the metal surface. Under
normal conditions, the amount of wear and resulting osteolysis associated with alumina
ceramic bearings has been very low.45 Alumina femoral heads exhibit great clinical outcomes
with only rare occasions of fracture. Since the introduction of alumina-zirconia composite
ceramics, the performance of ceramic bearings has substantially improved, with only a few
reported cases of fracture.
Wear features on the bearing surfaces of MOM THA implants differ between well-functioning
and high-wearing implants. Under well-functioning conditions, mild surface fatigue and
tribochemical reactions prevail.2 This means that fine wear debris is generated within an in
situ generated nano-crystalline subsurface zone, and wear is further reduced by the
formation of a carbonaceous tribofilm.48,49 Optically, the surface has an almost as-
manufactured polished appearance. The tribofilm may be visible by a slightly milky
appearance but most likely can be visualized only with the use of a scanning electron
microscope (SEM). Under adverse contact conditions, such as edge loading and micro-
separation, the nanocrystalline subsurface zone and the tribofilm are inconsequential,
whereas abrasion dominates. The resulting wear features are numerous grooves and
scratches, often within a confined stripe wear scar. This wear mechanism results in not only
increased material loss but also larger wear particles. In this circumstance, ALTRs are more
likely to occur.48,50 Wear features on femoral heads or condyles paired with polyethylene
liners usually are mild but may exhibit random grooves or scratches. These scratches likely
are not indicative of abrasion as the predominantly acting wear mechanism but rather a
random occurrence of an abrasive particle temporarily trapped between the articulating
surfaces without major implications on overall wear behavior.
Modes of Corrosion
Corrosion within modular junctions generally is attributed to mechanically assisted crevice
corrosion;3 however, the main problem leading to corrosion appears to be fretting corrosion,
which may be considered a corrosion mode falling under mechanically assisted crevice
corrosion (Resource 3). Recent research has shown that various corrosion modes can occur
simultaneously or in sequence.51 They generally can be differentiated as mechanically
dominated (eg, fretting) or chemically dominated.
Chemically dominated corrosion modes include pitting corrosion, etching, and phase
boundary corrosion. Chemical corrosion modes depend strongly on the presence of

preferential corrosion sites within the microstructure of the alloy9 and a change of the
chemical environment within the confined space of a modular junction.
Preferential corrosion sites include areas with inhomogeneous distribution of alloying
elements, phase boundaries, and hard phases.9,51 The change of the chemical environment
can be related to fretting currents, patient-specific differences in joint fluid composition,
inflammation, or cells within the joint environment.4-6,51 The exact mechanism of chemically
dominated corrosion and the effect of implant alloy microstructure are subjects of additional
research.
Damage Scoring
Material loss from wear or corrosion may lead to adverse tissue responses. Only a few
methods are available to monitor the effect of material loss in vivo via indirect measures, such
as blood metal levels52-54 or radiographic evaluation of bone resorption.55 These measures
may be misleading and may not necessarily reflect material loss from the implant, whereas
implant retrieval analysis allows for a precise measure of material loss; however, even such
retrospective analysis has limitations.
Quantification of material loss is not always possible because it requires specialized
equipment, such as a coordinate measuring machine (CMM). Therefore, semi-quantitative
scoring is an easy alternative that can be conducted with a stereomicroscope or other types of
digital light microscopes.
Damage can be categorized according to severity and areal coverage on specific implant
surfaces. Most scores rely on a simple scale, with 1 indicating no or minimal damage, 2
indicating mild damage, 3 indicating moderate damage, and 4 indicating severe damage.
Damage scoring is conducted primarily for implant surfaces that are difficult to measure
otherwise, such as backside damage of tibial or acetabular liners or modular taper
surfaces.15,56,57
A special focus has been placed on taper damage in recent years because of the acute
problem of mechanically assisted crevice corrosion–related ALTRs. Most scoring methods are
based on the Goldberg score that initially distinguished between corrosion and fretting
damage;57 however, currently, most studies use a modified version that involves a combined
fretting and corrosion score.51,58 With any damage scoring system, at least two observers
must be involved. Scores can be averaged, or the independent observers must reach a
consensus.

Microscopic Analysis and Qualitive Assessment of in Vivo Damage
Processes
Most damage features can be identified via light microscopy; however, certain damage
features can only be identified at higher magnification and require the use of a SEM, white
light interferometry, or other high-resolution techniques. Differentiation of damage features
related to fretting and corrosion requires through analysis at high magnifications,3,51 which is
one of the reasons separate visual scoring of fretting and corrosion has fallen out of favor. For
example, fretting damage and pitting corrosion features can be best identified in a SEM.
Accurate determination of the actual wear mechanisms and corrosion modes is essential to
take appropriate countermeasures.
Quantitative Damage Assessment
Quantitative assessment of in vivo material loss from the bearing surfaces of THA and TKA
implants is of great importance to understand the nature of the periprosthetic tissue
response. Although preclinical testing provides a great prediction tool for the wear
performance of a joint under ideal or worst-case conditions, the actual in vivo performance
must be monitored because unexpected events may result from the more complex chemical
environment or mechanical factors, such as subluxation, patient variability in gait, activity
levels, and loading.
Knowledge of actual volumetric material loss is important to define thresholds that indicate
the likelihood of an ALTR. Wear can be quantified in several manners depending on the type of
bearing surfaces.
In any case, actual measurements on retrievals will provide the best results. Wear can be
quantified via linear or volumetric measurements. Linear wear assessment is based on the
maximum penetration of the bearing surfaces. The advantage is that it can be conducted with
the use of simple tools, such as a caliper. For example, on polyethylene tibial liners, linear wear
rates correlate well with volumetric measurements; however, the room for error is
considerable. Linear wear is a good surrogate measurement for group comparisons but is
subject to high deviation on an individual basis.59 Therefore, volumetric wear assessment is
the most desirable but requires sophisticated equipment.
The most common approach to volumetric wear measurement is the use of a CMM with a
touch probe. This technique is commonly used for wear assessment of the spherical
articulating surfaces of THA implants; however, other techniques, such as out-of-roundness

machines or optical CMMs (using a laser or white light confocal sensor), also have been

Although all techniques provide the same information on material loss, additional information
may be gained, depending on the approach. Out-of-roundness machines can provide
additional roughness information, whereas optical CMM can be used for photorealistic
representation of the damaged surfaces. This feature is useful because it provides a map for
high-resolution imaging techniques (eg, SEM).51
Volumetric wear assessment of tibial inserts is more challenging because of the oddly shaped
geometry. Only a few studies have quantified volume loss from retrieved components using,
for example, an optical CMM with a laser sensor and an autonomous mathematic
reconstruction method.63 This approach has been used to determine the relationship between
surgical positioning of the implant and volumetric wear. For example, elevation of the joint line
has been shown to be associated with increased polyethylene wear56 (Figure 1).

Implant Material Characterization
Another important component of implant retrieval analysis is characterization of the actual
implant material. Material characterization aims to analyze the microstructure of a given

9/4/26, 10:24 AM
AAOS | Retrieval Analysis of Hip and Knee Prostheses
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001161
13/26

material. The applied methods vary among metals, ceramic, and polymers. Most studies do
not include thorough material characterization because most characterization methods are
destructive, which means that implants need to be sectioned for analysis, and it often is not
required, depending on the study goals; however, material characterization is required if the
failure mechanism is in doubt and may be related to the material properties.
For implants made from metal alloys, a metallographic analysis must be conducted.
Metallography entails sectioning of the implant, embedding the alloy section within a hard
resin, followed by grinding and polishing to a mirror finish. The implant microstructure can
be visualized via subsequent etching, with the exact protocol differing between common
implant alloys, such as CoCrMo, Ti6Al4V, and stainless steels. Etched metal alloy samples can
be analyzed under a microscope to visualize grain size and shape.
Grains are individual crystals that comprise the metal implant. In addition, an alloy may be
composed of different phases. Phases are areas with different atomic packing orders that
directly influence the mechanical properties of the allow. For example, Ti6Al4V is a biphasic
alloy consisting of the hexagonal close packed alpha phase (hcp) and the body centered
cubic (bcc) beta phase. CoCrMo consists only of a single phase (face centered cubic, or fcc)
but also can contain so-called hard phases that behave differently from metals, such as
carbides and intermetallic phases. The presence of hard phases depends on the carbon
content within the alloy and the type of heat treatments that were applied. Metallographic
analysis will reveal the microstructure that is present in a specific case, which may differ
among manufacturers and also within the same manufacturer.
Implant alloys may differ depending on suppliers and lot numbers. In addition, the type of
manufacturing process (cast, wrought, powder metallurgy, additive manufacturing/three-
dimensional printing) results in very different microstructures despite identical chemical
composition.
Specific microstructural features may be beneficial or harmful depending on the application.
For example, the presence of hard phases may be beneficial to reduce wear rate in MOM
bearings (especially if three-body wear occurs) but may be harmful in modular junctions by
offering preferential corrosion sites.9,64 In some cases, failure of an individual implant or a
specific implant design may be directly related to flaws within the microstructure.
High-resolution crystallographic analysis methods can be applied for additional
microstructural characterization of metal alloys. These methods include electron backscatter
diffraction in combination with SEM or electron diffraction pattern analysis in combination
with transmission electron microscopy.

The same tools also can be applied for ceramic implant components because ceramic and
metals are both crystalline materials; however, material analysis of ceramics rarely is
conducted because of the low incidence of material failure and the difficult process of
sample preparation.
Ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene is a partially crystalline material consisting of
macromolecules. Therefore, a different tool set is required for analysis. Ideally, ultra-high–
molecular-weight polyethylene is analyzed via Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy.32,37,38
The infrared spectrum is very sensitive to specific functional groups, which are distinct in most
polymers. Fine changes within the infrared fingerprint allow for the determination of the
oxidation index, crystallinity, and protein absorption. Analysis can be conducted on the surface
via attenuated total reflection or, most commonly, by using the infrared transmission mode of
thin cross-section samples. Alternatively, Raman spectroscopy can be used to characterize
ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene and for in vivo alteration of its chemical structure.
Raman spectroscopy is ideal for the analysis of surfaces without any need of sample
preparation; however, care must be taken to ensure that the laser intensity selected is not too
high because it may alter the ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene structure (eg, local
melting) and, therefore, generate artifacts. Tracking in vivo oxidation of ultra-high–molecular-
weight polyethylene components is important to predict its potential lifetime.
Tissue Retrieval Analysis
The study of periprosthetic and remote tissues can enhance implant retrieval analysis and add
key information to the understanding of implant failure.24 Excessive generation of wear
particles and the release of metal ions may induce adverse local reactions in the periprosthetic
tissues.21
Periprosthetic Tissue Analysis
The type and occurrence of local adverse tissue reactions differ depending on the nature of
the wear particles, especially with respect to their size.50 In periprosthetic tissues, the cellular
responses to particulates from wear and corrosion are driven by the innate (nonspecific) or
adaptive (specific) immune system (Figure 2). The cellular response linked to the innate
immunologic response is characterized by chronic inflammation with a cellular infiltrate
dominated by macrophages and foreign body giant cells (groups of fused macrophages) that
can form particle-induced granulomas. In reaction to implant debris, macrophages increase

Semiquantitative Scoring of Cellular Infiltrates
To compare the histopathologic features of retrieved periprosthetic tissues, a semiquantitative
scoring method can be used by experienced histopathologists.65 Using light microscopy at
magnifications ranging from ×50 to ×500, hematoxylin-eosin stained sections can be scored for
the presence of necrosis, inflammatory exudate, and cell types (lymphocyte, plasma cells,
eosinophils, polymorphonuclear leukocytes, macrophages, and foreign body giant cells).
Grading systems rely on a simple scale, with 1 being rare, 2 being mild, 3 being moderate, and
4 being severe.
The ALVAL scoring method is another useful tool to compare the degree of tissue reactions
among study samples.20 This method is validated in the literature and involves the sum of
grades for synovial lining integrity, inflammatory cell infiltrates, and tissue organization. With
this methodology, scores can range from 0 to 10. Low ALVAL scores range from 0 to 4,
moderate ALVAL scores range from 5 to 8, and high ALVAL scores range from 9 to 10. For any
scoring method used, multiple sites from several tissue samples for each case should be
analyzed.
Immunohistochemistry
Immunohistochemistry of the periprosthetic tissues allows for immunophenotyping of cells by
identifying cell surface molecules via cluster of differentiation (CD) protocols. CD molecules are
classified by the reference monoclonal antibodies to which they bind. CD3, CD20, and CD68
are commonly used in the analysis of periprosthetic tissue because they delineate T
lymphocytes, B lymphocytes, and activated macrophages, respectively. In lymphocyte-
dominated ALTRs, the lymphocytic infiltrate is dominated by CD3+ T cells in a perivascular and
diffuse distribution, whereas CD20+ B cells are mostly limited to perivascular sites.8 Further
phenotyping with additional CD markers has identified that among the CD3+ T lymphocyte
subpopulation are CD4+ helper T cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. Classifying the cell

Elemental Identification of Particles
For elemental identification of particles within the tissues, serial sections adjacent to the
hematoxylin-eosin section are cut from the paraffin block and mounted unstained on high-
purity carbon planchets. The disks are analyzed via back-scattered SEM with energy dispersive
x-ray spectroscopy at magnifications ranging from ×1,000 to ×20,000. Individual particles can
be located and their elemental composition can be determined via energy dispersive x-ray
spectroscopy.
This technique allows for identification of metal alloy particles as small as 50 nm in size.
Multiple fields should be analyzed for each sample. Only intracellular particles should be
included, to exclude the possibility of extraneous particulate contaminants (ie, stainless-steel
particles from sectioning tools).
Remote Tissue Analysis
Analysis of postmortem retrieved tissues has shown that particles from joint prostheses can
migrate from their site of generation to remote organs and bone marrow.14 The methodology
outlined earlier for periprosthetic tissue analysis is easily adapted to study remote organ
tissue samples.
Assessment of Osseointegration
Biologic fixation is the attachment of a porous coated or surface-structured implant to the
skeleton by bone and occurs via bone ingrowth/ongrowth and osseointegration. The process
of bone ingrowth and ongrowth resembles fracture healing via the mechanism of
intramembranous ossification (mesenchymal cells to bone).
Surgeons often use the term osseointegration to indicate the radiographic appearance of the
bone-implant interface; however, osseointegration actually is a histologic term implying the
bonding of bone with an implant so that no gap between the bone and implant can be
observed at the highest magnification.
One method to study the bone-implant interface in retrieved implants is undecalcified plastic
embedding. This method is particularly effective in the evaluation of postmortem retrieved
